subject: math
title: Sorting and Graphs: Sorting Rules, Tally Marks and Pictographs
seo_title: Grade 1 Sorting and Graphs Worksheets: Tally Marks and Pictographs (Free, Answer Key, Ontario)
standard_text: Display sets of data, using one-to-one correspondence, in concrete graphs and pictographs with proper sources, titles, and labels
meta_desc: Free Grade 1 math worksheets on sorting and graphs for the Ontario curriculum: sort by colour, shape or size and name the rule, read tally marks in bundles of 5, read pictographs where 1 picture = 1, order from greatest to least, and compare. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Sort it, count it, show it, then ask what it tells you.
key_sub: A sorting rule must fit every thing in the group. A tally bundle is 5. In a Grade 1 pictograph, 1 picture = 1. How many more means compare; altogether means add.
body_html:
The big idea

Data is information we collect, like votes in a class survey. First we sort things into groups. Then we count each group with tally marks. Then we show the data in a pictograph. Last, we ask what the graph tells us.

Sort and name the rule

A sorting rule tells how things go together. We can sort by colour, by shape or by size. To find the rule, look at every thing in one group. What is the same for all of them?

Tally marks: bundles of 5

Make one mark for each thing. The 5th mark goes across the first 4. That makes a bundle of 5. To read a tally, count the bundles by 5s, then count on the single marks.

Pictographs: 1 picture = 1

In a Grade 1 pictograph, one picture stands for one thing. A good graph has a title at the top, labels for the rows, a key, and a source that tells where the data came from. Put your finger on the label. Then count the pictures in that row only.

Order from greatest to least

The greatest number is the longest row. The least number is the shortest row. Find the greatest first, then the next, then the least.

Greatest to least

Apple 7, Banana 3, Grapes 5. Put them in order from greatest to least.

7 is the greatest. 5 is next. 3 is the least.

Answer: Apple, Grapes, Banana

Compare and answer questions

How many more or how many fewer means compare. Match the pictures one to one, or take the smaller number away from the bigger one. Altogether means add.

How many more?

How many more votes did Apple get than Grapes?

Apple 7, Grapes 5. 2 stars are left over. 7 − 5 = 2.

Answer: 2 more votes

How many altogether?

How many votes were there altogether?

Apple 7, Banana 3, Grapes 5. 7 + 3 + 5 = 15.

Answer: 15 votes

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Naming a rule that fits only some thingsCheck every thing in the group
Counting a bundle of tally marks as 44 marks and 1 line across is 5
Reading the row above or belowPut your finger on the label first, then read that row
Writing the order backwardsGreatest to least starts with the longest row
Adding when it asks how many moreHow many more or fewer means compare, so subtract
Mixing up the title and the sourceThe title is at the top; the source is at the bottom

faq.q: What do Grade 1 students learn about data in the Ontario math curriculum?
faq.a: They sort things by one attribute and name the sorting rule, collect data with tally marks, and show it in concrete graphs and pictographs where one picture stands for one. They also order the categories from greatest to least and answer questions about the data.

faq.q: How do you teach tally marks in Grade 1?
faq.a: Make one mark for each thing, and draw the 5th mark across the first 4 to make a bundle of 5. To read a tally, count the bundles by 5s and then count on the single marks, so 1 bundle and 2 marks is 7.

faq.q: What is a pictograph in Grade 1 math?
faq.a: It is a graph that uses pictures, with one picture for each thing (one-to-one correspondence). A complete pictograph has a title, labels, a key and a source that says where the data came from.

faq.q: How can I practise sorting and graphing with my Grade 1 child at home?
faq.a: Sort laundry, toys or snacks and ask “What is your rule?” Then ask the family a question, such as their favourite fruit, keep a tally, and ask which got the most and how many more.

sets.title: Compare and answer questions: word problems

items.q: Ms. Lee’s class voted for a favourite fruit. How many more votes did Banana get than Grapes?
items.e: Count the circles. Each one is 1. Banana: 7. Grapes: 2. Match them up one to one. 5 are left over: 7 − 2 = 5. The answer is 5 more votes.

items.q: Room 5 asked how students get to school. How many students walk or come by car?
items.e: Count the tally marks. A bundle is 5. Walk: 8. Car: 3. Add the two rows: 8 + 3 = 11 students.

items.q: Our class kept a weather chart for 2 weeks. How many more days were snowy than cloudy?
items.e: Count the squares. Each one is 1. Snowy: 7. Cloudy: 4. Match them up one to one. 3 are left over: 7 − 4 = 3. The answer is 3 more days.

items.q: Ms. Lee’s class voted for a favourite fruit. How many fewer votes did Grapes get than Apple?
items.e: Count the tally marks. A bundle is 5. Apple: 6. Grapes: 4. Match them up one to one. 2 are left over: 6 − 4 = 2. The answer is 2 fewer votes.

items.q: Room 5 asked how students get to school. How many students are in the survey?
items.e: Count the circles. Each one is 1. Walk: 5. Car: 4. Bike: 7. Add all three rows: 5 + 4 + 7 = 16 students. (There are 3 rows, but the answer is the number of students.)

items.q: Room 3 asked what students play at recess. How many more students picked the swings than tag?
items.e: Count the tally marks. A bundle is 5. Swings: 3. Tag: 1. Match them up one to one. 2 are left over: 3 − 1 = 2. The answer is 2 more students.

items.q: Ms. Lee’s class voted for a favourite fruit. How many votes did Grapes and Orange get altogether?
items.e: Count the squares. Each one is 1. Grapes: 7. Orange: 8. Add the two rows: 7 + 8 = 15 votes.

items.q: Room 5 asked how students get to school. How many fewer students walk than take the bus?

items.q: We counted birds at the school feeder. How many more cardinals than sparrows did we see?

items.q: Ms. Lee’s class voted for a favourite fruit. How many more votes does Orange need to tie with Banana?
items.e: Count the tally marks. A bundle is 5. Banana: 9. Orange: 3. Orange needs to go from 3 up to 9. Count on from 3 to 9, or 9 − 3 = 6. So Orange needs 6 more votes.

items.q: Room 5 asked how students get to school. How many fewer students walk than come by car?
